title_eng: Atrial Fibrillation Identification Using CNNs Based on Genomic Data
abstract:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common cardiac arrhythmia and a major cardiovascular disease epidemic of the 21st 
century. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial as AF often progresses without symptoms. This study aims to identify 
AF using genome-wide association studies and convolutional neural networks (CNN). Genomic data from 6,358 individu -
als were used to develop a CNN model, with L2 regularization applied to prevent overfitting. The L2-regularized CNN 
significantly outperformed the regular CNN across various p-value thresholds. For instance, at p < 0.0001, the L2-reg -
ularized CNN achieved an accuracy of 0.731 ± 0.071 compared to 0.703 ± 0.055 for the regular CNN. At p < 0.001, the 
L2-regularized CNN showed an accuracy of 0.630 ± 0.089, while the regular CNN had 0.577 ± 0.095. This demonstrates 
a notable improvement in model performance with L2 regularization. Although the regular CNN showed higher accuracy 
in some scenarios, such as achieving 0.984 ± 0.015 at p < 0.01 compared to 0.970 ± 0.020 for the L2-regularized CNN, 
the performance difference between the models decreased as the p-value threshold became more stringent. Overall, L2 
regularization not only improved the model’s performance and stability but also reduced the performance gap between 
the models under stricter p-value conditions. These findings highlight that L2-regularized CNNs can significantly enhance 
performance in genomic studies, offering a more effective alternative to traditional polygenic risk score methods for AF 
identification study.

procedures, making them well-suited for analyzing high-
dimensional biological data [ 9]. Nevertheless, genomic 
datasets are vast and information-rich, posing inherent risks 
of overfitting for CNN models [ 10]. Therefore, it is crucial 
to employ regularization techniques to ensure generaliza -
tion performance. L2 regularization, which reduces model 
weights to prevent overfitting in high-dimensional data, is a 
widely adopted approach [11, 12].

The study aimed to develop a CNN-based deep neural 
network model for whole-genome analysis. The goal is to 
predict AF risk groups with greater accuracy and general -
ization capability than existing PRS models. We use GWAS 
data from patients with AF and healthy controls to opti -
mize the CNN model’s architecture and hyperparameters. 
L2 regularization and other techniques will be employed 
to address overfitting, and the model’s performance will 
be validated through cross-validation and evaluation on 
separate test datasets. Furthermore, by analyzing the SNP 
features captured by the model, we aim to elucidate the 
underlying mechanisms of AF pathogenesis.
2 Materials and Methods
Figure 1 illustrates the overall process of this study. Four 
independent GWAS cohorts from South Korea were used, 
and AF-related SNPs were filtered based on the AF-related 
SNP list from the BioBank Japan cohort. These SNPs were 
then applied to a machine-learning model to diagnose AF. 
The model’s performance was analyzed under various 
p-value thresholds and compared to the traditional GWAS 
analysis technique, PRS.
2.1 Dataset
This study used whole-genome data from 6,358 individuals 
collected from four independent cohorts. The patient with AF 
group comprised 200 participants from the Korean AF Net-
work cohort and 672 participants from the Severance Hos -
pital cohort at Yonsei University (Yonsei AF cohort; Seoul, 
Republic of Korea), totaling 872 patients. The control group 
comprised 3,700 individuals from a health examinee study 
cohort and 1,786 individuals from the Korean Multi-Rural 
Communities Cohort (KoGES-MRC cohort), totaling 5,486 
controls. The control data were sourced from the Korean 
Genome and Epidemiology Study (KoGES), funded by the 
National Research Institute of Health. The KoGES includes 
several large-scale population-based cohorts and has been 
used for various epidemiological studies on chronic dis -
eases. KoGES recruited individuals over 40 years old 
between 2001 and 2013 to identify genetic and environmen-
tal factors associated with chronic diseases such as diabetes, 
hypertension, obesity, hyperlipidemia, metabolic syndrome, 
and cardiovascular disease [ 13]. This study used data from 
the Korean Multi-Rural Communities Cohort study and 
the KoGES Health Examinees (HEXA) study. The Korean 
Multi-Rural Communities Cohort (KoGES-HEXA cohort), 
established in 2004, aims to identify cardiovascular risk 
factors among Koreans. This multi-center cohort recruited 
9,697 participants aged 40 years and older from three rural 
areas between January 2005 and August 2009 [ 14]. The 
KoGES HEXA study collected data from 167,169 partici -
pants aged 40–69 years between 2004 and 2013. Follow-up 
was conducted through both active and passive methods. 
Active follow-up was initiated in 2012 and continued until 
2015, while passive follow-up primarily involved data link-
ages with the National Death Certificate, National Cancer 
Registry, and National Health Insurance Claim data [15].
All participants were of Korean ethnicity, and the genomic 
data included 531,766 SNPs across chromosomes 1–22. 
Genotyping was performed using the Affymetrix Human 
SNP 6.0 GeneChip array (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, Califor-
nia, USA) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Table 1 
provides the demographic information of the patients with 
AF and control groups. The mean age of the patient group 
was 50.24 ± 8.37 years, while it was 55.61 ± 8.57 years for 
the control group. The proportion of males was higher in

2.2 Pre-Processing
For the GWAS analysis, we used the AF analysis results from 
the BioBank Japan cohort, sourced from a previously pub -
lished GWAS study [ 16]. The dataset comprised 471,462 
mapped SNPs. SNPs were extracted based on p-value thresh-
olds of 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, which are more generous than 
the traditional GWAS significance level of p < 5 × 10− 8 [17], 
based on previous study [ 18]. The genotype of a bi-allelic 
SNP can either be homozygous or heterozygous, represented 
by pairs of alleles (e.g., AA and aa for homozygous major and 
minor genotypes, and Aa for heterozygous genotypes). Since 
SNP genotypes are categorical, any encoding scheme capable 
of distinguishing between different genotypes can be chosen. 
A common method is minor allele encoding, where genotypes 
AA, Aa, and aa are encoded as “0,” “1,” and “2,” respectively. 
In our study, missing values were encoded as “-9” (Fig. 2) [19]. 
The binary labels indicating the presence (1) or absence (0) of 
AF were assigned to patients and normal controls, respectively.
2.3 Model Development and Optimization
The baseline model for AF identification comprised stacked 
deep convolutional layers and fully connected layers. The 
deep convolutional layers consisted of 1D convolution lay -
ers with dropout, while the fully connected layers included 
one hidden layer and an output layer. Hyperparameters were 
optimized using Bayesian optimization, selecting values that 
yielded the best accuracy during cross-validation [20]. Tuning 
was performed within the following ranges: number of convo-
lutional layers (3–9), number of convolutional filters (4–256), 
filter size (2–4), dropout rate (0.05–0.55), number of nodes in 
the fully connected layer (4–256), and batch size (8–32). All 
the stacked deep convolutional layers shared the same archi-
tecture and settings. The activation functions were ReLU for 
the convolutional and fully connected layers, and Sigmoid for 
the output layer. In the L2-regularized model, L2 regularization 
(λ = 0.001) was applied to all layers of the baseline model.
2.4 Model Training
The binary cross-entropy function served as the loss function 
for model training. We employed the Adam optimizer [ 21] 
with a learning rate set to 0.005. The training was performed 
for 1000 epochs. To prevent overfitting during training, we 
adopted an approach where we selected the model at the epoch 
with the minimum validation loss as the optimal model [22].
2.5 Validation
We employed 5-fold cross-validation, ensuring that the ratio 
of controls to patients in each fold matched the overall ratio 
in the entire dataset [23]. Within each fold, 20% of the train-
ing data was randomly selected as the validation set. To assess 
the reproducibility of model performance, the cross-validation 
process was repeated five times. During each cross-validation 
iteration, we assessed accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive 
predictive value, area under the receiver operating characteris-
tic curve (AUROC), and area under the precision-recall curve 
(AUPRC).
2.6 Polygenic Risk Score
A PRS is a metric used to predict an individual’s susceptibility 
to complex genetic diseases. PRS is computed as a weighted 
sum of the risk alleles an individual carries for various genetic 
variants (SNPs) associated with the disease of interest. Higher
